title: DSA: timed mock habits (25-minute problem)
seriesDescription: Topic-by-topic JEE-style quizzes for the backend and AI-engineering interview roadmap: integer, assertion-reason, matrix match, fill-in-the-blanks, short code writing, plus multi-correct questions. Language core, concurrency, DSA, web frameworks, data access, databases, messaging, resilience, security, testing, system design, LLM and agent engineering.
description: How to run one problem in 25 minutes: clarify, brute force first, narrate, choose edge cases, write your own tests, and use constraints to pick complexity.
source: Cracking the Coding Interview (McDowell); Tech Interview Handbook; LeetCode constraints-to-complexity discussions; interview experience write-ups

questions.prompt: In a 25-minute round you spend 4 minutes clarifying, 6 minutes agreeing an approach out loud and 10 minutes coding. How many minutes are left for testing and fixing?
questions.explanation: 25 - 4 - 6 - 10 = 5. A rough split is 3-5 clarify, 5-7 approach, 10-12 code and 5 test. If coding is running long, say so and prioritise a working core over polish.

questions.prompt: The input has n = 10^5 elements and your idea is O(n^2). Assuming about 10^8 simple operations per second, roughly how many seconds will it take?
questions.explanation: n^2 = 10^10 operations, divided by 10^8 per second is 100 seconds, far too slow. An n of 10^5 signals you need O(n log n) or O(n). The 10^8 rate is a rule of thumb, not a guarantee.

questions.prompt: Five minutes in, you have no optimal idea. What is the best next move?

options.text: State the brute force and its complexity aloud, then find the bottleneck.
options.why: Correct: it shows progress, gives the interviewer something to steer, and exposes the repeated work.

options.text: Stay silent until the right idea arrives, so you never say anything wrong at all.
options.why: Silence gives the interviewer no signal and no chance to hint.

options.text: Ask the interviewer to name the algorithm, then implement it from memory.
options.why: Asking for the answer outright ends the evaluation; ask a targeted question instead.

options.text: Switch to a different, easier problem without telling anyone.
options.why: Abandoning the question silently looks like giving up.

questions.explanation: A correct brute force beats a half-built optimal solution. Then improve it: ask what work repeats, and what data structure removes it.

questions.prompt: The prompt says: "find the duplicate numbers in an array". You start typing code immediately. What did you skip?

options.text: Clarifying inputs, constraints and an example, such as size, ranges and return type.
options.why: Correct: the answer changes with the constraints, e.g. O(1) space is possible for values in 1..n.

options.text: Writing the unit tests first, because every interview requires strict test-driven development.
options.why: Tests are good, but they are not the usual first step in a timed round.

options.text: Choosing between Java and Python for the rest of the interview before reading further.
options.why: Choose a language early, but that is not what the missing step is here.

options.text: Declaring the final Big-O before you have a design, as the first sentence.
options.why: Complexity comes after you have an approach to analyse.

questions.explanation: Questions to ask: size and range, duplicates allowed, sorted, memory limits, return all or one, invalid input.

questions.prompt: A problem states n <= 2 * 10^5. What does that most strongly suggest about the target time complexity?

options.text: O(n log n) or O(n); nested loops over n would be too slow.
options.why: Correct: 2*10^5 squared is 4*10^10 operations.

options.text: O(n^2) is fine, because computers perform billions of operations per second now.
options.why: Even at 10^8 to 10^9 simple operations per second, 4*10^10 takes far too long.

options.text: O(2^n) with pruning, because the input is bounded by a constant of about 2*10^5.
options.why: Exponential only works for n up to roughly 20-25.

options.text: O(n!) with memoisation, as the bound is generous enough to permit it.
options.why: Factorial only works for n up to roughly 10-11, even with pruning.

questions.explanation: n <= 20 suggests bitmask or backtracking, n <= 10^3 to 10^4 allows O(n^2), n up to 10^5-10^6 needs O(n log n) or O(n).

questions.prompt: You wrote merge(intervals) for merging overlapping closed intervals. Select all that apply: which inputs belong in your own test cases?

options.text: An empty list.
options.why: Correct: the minimum input often crashes code that reads intervals[0].

options.text: Touching intervals such as [1,2] and [2,3].
options.why: Correct: the boundary decides between < and <=.

options.text: A nested interval such as [1,10] and [2,3].
options.why: Correct: it checks that the end uses max, not the latest end.

options.text: Unsorted input such as [[8,10],[1,3],[2,6]].
options.why: Correct: it proves the sort is really there.

options.text: Only the sample from the problem statement.
options.why: The sample is written to pass; it rarely probes boundaries.

options.text: One random array of 10^6 values and nothing else.
options.why: A single large input cannot be checked by hand and misses targeted boundaries.

questions.explanation: Good habit: empty/minimum, single element, boundaries, duplicates, already sorted vs reversed, and one tiny case you can verify by hand.

questions.prompt: Complete the order of a well-run round.
questions.text: Clarify the inputs, state a {1} solution, give its {2}, then optimise; after coding, {3} an example by hand.
questions.explanation: Stating brute force first banks partial credit and creates a baseline. Tracing a small input through your code finds off-by-one errors before the interviewer does.

questions.prompt: Match each situation in a timed round with the best habit.

left.text: You are unsure whether the array can contain negatives
Your dry run reveals a bug
You can think of two approaches
Time is almost out and the code is half done

right.text: Ask a clarifying question before coding on
Say it aloud, name the cause and make a minimal fix
Compare the trade-offs and agree one with the interviewer
State what remains, the complexity, and how you would finish
Delete everything and restart in silence

questions.explanation: Interviewers grade the process: fixing a visible bug calmly is positive, restarting silently is not. Narrating the trade-off between two approaches is often worth more than coding the second one.

questions.assertion: You should narrate your reasoning while you solve the problem.
questions.reason: Interviewers can only give hints or award credit for thinking they can hear.

whys.a: Right: R is the reason narration helps.

questions.explanation: Short, structured narration works best: what you are doing, why, and what the complexity will be. Do not narrate every keystroke.

questions.assertion: Writing your own test cases before the interviewer asks is a strong positive signal.
questions.reason: Interviewers stop caring about correctness once the algorithm has the optimal complexity.

whys.a: R is false, so it cannot explain A.
whys.c: Right: A is true, but R is false because a wrong optimal-looking solution still fails.

questions.explanation: Optimal complexity with a wrong boundary condition is still a wrong answer. Always trace at least one normal and one edge case.

questions.prompt: Finishing the code with minutes to spare.
questions.assertion: If the solution has the optimal complexity, testing it is unnecessary.
questions.reason: Off-by-one errors and empty-input crashes are common, and a short dry run usually catches them.

whys.a: A is false, so R cannot explain it.
whys.d: Right: A is false, and R is true, which is exactly why a dry run is needed.

questions.explanation: Use the leftover time for one normal case, one boundary case, and a note on complexity.

questions.prompt: In Python, write three assert statements for merge(intervals) (which returns a list of [start, end] lists): an empty input, touching intervals [1,2] and [2,3], and a nested pair [1,10] and [2,3].
questions.explanation: Pick expected values you can verify by hand. Input order matters in the touching case: [2,3] first would test the sort as well. Frameworks like pytest.mark.parametrize group these, but plain asserts are fine in an interview.

questions.prompt: True or false: if you realise halfway that your approach is wrong, the best move is to silently restart so you do not look unsure.

options.text: True
options.why: Silence hides your thinking.

options.text: False
options.why: Correct: say "this approach breaks when ... so I will switch to ..."; changing course openly shows good judgement.

questions.explanation: Recovering visibly is a positive signal; hiding the pivot wastes time and removes any chance of a hint.
